lessonRef.unitTitle: Summary and Theme: Saying What a Story Means
lessonRef.focus: retrieving summary, theme, and literary evidence together
lessonRef.title: Retrieval and assessment preparation: retrieving summary, theme, and literary evidence together

studentTask.text: This Grade 4 lesson develops retrieving summary, theme, and literary evidence together within the unit “Summary and Theme: Saying What a Story Means.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's retrieval and assessment preparation work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
In a village at the edge of a wide field there lived a boy named Corin, who was known for one thing: he counted the crows.

Every morning he sat on the stone wall and counted them as they crossed from the woods to the field. Thirty-one. Twenty-eight. Thirty-three. The villagers laughed at him, kindly at first and then less kindly, because a boy of his age might have been mending nets or carrying water.

"What good is the number of crows?" the miller asked.

"I do not know yet," Corin said. "I only know it."

One autumn the count began to fall. Twenty-two. Nineteen. Fourteen. Corin told the miller, who told him crows were crows. He told the baker, who told him to carry water.

On the ninth day he counted four, and the four did not land in the field at all. They circled once and flew on toward the hills.

Corin walked to the field himself. He knelt and dug into the soil with his hands, and what he found there were grubs, thick and pale, more than he could hold, chewing at the roots of the winter wheat.

The crows had not abandoned the field. They had eaten what they could and gone looking for a field that still had something left in it.

Corin ran back to the village. This time the miller listened, because the number four is a hard thing to argue with when you have been told about thirty-one for two years.

The villagers turned the soil and saved most of the crop.

Afterward the baker asked Corin how he had known.

"I did not know," Corin said. "I counted. Knowing came later, and it could only come because I had been counting all along, back when it meant nothing at all."

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “The Boy Who Counted Crows”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what retrieving summary, theme, and literary evidence together asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “The Boy Who Counted Crows,” then answer: Audit your readiness on retrieving summary, theme, and literary evidence together. Which criterion is secure, which needs practice, and what source-based practice will close the gap?

Deliverable: Grade 4: a readiness audit with one completed practice item drawn from the reading; write two connected paragraphs.

Evidence requirement: Use two exact details. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If retrieving summary, theme, and literary evidence together is not yet secure, return to “The Boy Who Counted Crows” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply retrieving summary, theme, and literary evidence together to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “The Boy Who Counted Crows.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
